lessons.title: Why water quality matters
lessons.html:
Water is the fish's whole world

Fish and shellfish live, breathe, eat and get rid of waste in the water. If the water is bad, they get stressed, stop eating, get sick and can die. Most problems on a fish farm start with poor water quality. Checking the water every day is one of your most important jobs.

The main water quality factors

FactorWhat it isWhy it matters
Dissolved oxygenOxygen in the water that fish breathe through their gillsToo little and fish suffocate
TemperatureHow warm or cold the water isControls feeding, growth and how much oxygen the water holds
pHHow acid or alkaline the water isVery high or low pH harms gills and makes ammonia more poisonous
AmmoniaWaste from fish gills and rotting feedPoisonous to fish
NitriteMade from ammonia by bacteriaPoisonous; stops blood carrying oxygen
TurbidityHow cloudy the water isMud can block gills; very green water can crash and use up oxygen
SalinityHow salty the water isMarine animals need the right salt level; freshwater fish need fresh water

The right level for each factor depends on the species. Your farm will have a chart with the safe range for each one. Learn it and keep a copy near the testing kit.

lessons.title: Oxygen, temperature and waste
lessons.html:
Dissolved oxygen

Oxygen gets into water from the air, from waterfalls and aerators, and from water plants and algae during the day. At night, algae, fish and bacteria all use oxygen, and none is made. So oxygen is lowest just before sunrise.

Signs of low oxygen

  • Fish come to the surface and gulp air (gasping).
  • Fish gather where fresh water enters.
  • Fish stop eating.
  • Sudden deaths, often of the biggest fish first.

What to do

  1. Tell your supervisor immediately. It is an emergency.
  2. Switch on extra aerators or increase water flow as instructed.
  3. Stop feeding until oxygen is back to normal.

Temperature

Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water. In hot weather oxygen problems are more common, and fish need more oxygen because they are more active. Check temperature at the same times each day. Write it down.

Ammonia and nitrite

Fish give off ammonia. Leftover feed and dead fish also make ammonia as they rot. In ponds and biological filters, good bacteria change ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate, which is much less harmful.

How to keep ammonia low

  • Do not overfeed. Feed only what the fish eat.
  • Remove dead fish every day.
  • Keep filters clean and working.
  • Do not crowd too many fish into one tank.
  • Do not wash biological filters with chlorinated tap water; it kills the good bacteria.

lessons.title: Testing water and keeping records
lessons.html:
How to test water

Farms use different tools:

  • Thermometer: for temperature.
  • Oxygen meter: a probe that reads dissolved oxygen. Keep the probe clean and calibrate it as the instructions say.
  • pH meter or test kit.
  • Test kits for ammonia and nitrite: you add drops or tablets to a water sample and compare the colour with a chart.
  • Secchi disc: a black and white disc lowered into a pond to see how cloudy the water is.
  • Refractometer: for salinity on marine farms.

Steps for a test kit

  1. Rinse the test tube with the water you are testing.
  2. Take the sample from the place the farm procedure says, not from the surface only.
  3. Follow the kit instructions exactly: number of drops, waiting time.
  4. Read the colour in good daylight.
  5. Write down the result straight away.
  6. Wash the tube and close the kit. Some test chemicals are harmful; keep them away from food and children and wash your hands after use.

Records

Write down: date, time, tank or pond number, each reading, and your name. Records show changes over time. A slow rise in ammonia or a drop in morning oxygen warns you of a problem before fish start dying.

When a result is outside the safe range

Test again to check. If it is still wrong, tell your supervisor at once. Do not add chemicals to the water unless your supervisor tells you to.

Key points

  • Most fish farm problems start with poor water quality.
  • Oxygen is lowest just before sunrise; gasping fish are an emergency.
  • Ammonia from fish waste, leftover feed and dead fish is poisonous.
  • Do not overfeed, remove dead fish and keep filters working.
  • Test water the same way at the same times and record every result.
